paras: The threatened lynching of Samuel B. Goode took place in New York City on August 22, 1885, when a crowd yelled "Lynch him" and "Kill the black hound" as Goode, a Black man accused of stabbing Policeman James North to death, was taken to the Tombs. Goode was not harmed and was committed without bail, and a coroner's jury later found that North died of a stab wound inflicted by him. The New York papers dwelt more on the police captain's view, echoed by the Dispatch and the Black New York Freeman, that North provoked the fight by slapping, kicking and clubbing Goode.

North, 23, patrolled Wall Street and Broadway for the Old Slip precinct. Goode, also named in the papers as Samuel B. Booker and William Booker Goode, was assistant janitor at 20 Nassau Street. The Sun said he came from Virginia, the Washington Evening Star that he was a native of Washington.

Near midnight on August 21, North was talking with Mary Ann Masterson, a young woman about to sail for Ireland, when Goode spoke to her. Masterson testified that Goode insulted her and that North slapped and kicked him; the Dispatch said North also clubbed him and made no attempt to arrest him. Witnesses said Goode came back, the two men scuffled, and North was stabbed twice in the throat and died on the sidewalk within minutes.

Goode fled down Pine Street and was arrested near Water Street by Policeman William J. Newell, who told the inquest he was "followed by a howling mob." A wire account quoted Goode on his arrest: "I am as good as a white man, and want to be protected." The next morning, as he was moved from the Old Slip station house to the Tombs, a crowd surrounded him and called for his lynching, according to a New York dispatch in the Washington Critic. No attack on him is reported, and the fuller New York accounts of that day do not mention the crowd.

Justice Power committed Goode for examination, and Masterson was held as a witness in the House of Detention. North was buried at Flatbush Cemetery on August 24. At the inquest on August 26 the coroner's jury found that North died from a stab wound inflicted by Goode, who was committed without bail.

A physician reported human blood on a knife found in a Pine Street areaway. On September 11 Goode was arraigned in General Sessions, and his trial was set for September 21 over his counsel's objection. No report of the trial's outcome, or of action against the crowd, appears in the coverage.

The lynch cries reached print only in the Critic's brief dispatch, headed "Lynch Law Sought in New York." The New York Sun's first report, "Murder of a Policeman," called Goode "a surly colored man" and a "low-browed black negro." A day later the Sun printed his denial and Captain Caffrey's view that North "shouldn't have slapped and kicked the negro the way he did."

The Dispatch headlined "The Club of a Hasty Policeman, and the Knife of a Negro" and said the evidence "shows that the officer provoked the crime." Three weeks later the same paper wrote that the case "was either a murder or a justifiable homicide." Wire versions elsewhere, such as the Narragansett Herald's, led with Goode's alleged insult and called Masterson "the unfortunate cause of the tragedy."

The New York Freeman, a Black weekly, answered with an editorial, "The Colored Murderer." It said the policeman had no right to club a man he should have arrested and that Goode "acted largely in self-defense," but left judgment to the courts. The Freeman did not mention the crowd and urged the police to be "more courteous."

Masterson and other witnesses said Goode returned after being slapped and kicked and attacked North, two quoting him as saying "I'll fix you." The Sun's first report said he admitted stabbing North because North shoved him. In jail Goode said North clubbed and kicked him without cause and that he ran away, carried no knife and stabbed no one. Reports also differ on the hour, his age and his home.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Samuel B. Goode
bases: A crowd surrounded Goode, a Black prisoner accused of killing a policeman, during his transfer to the Tombs and yelled "Lynch him" and "Kill the black hound" (A1); no attack followed, so it is a threatened lynching, preceded by a policeman's slapping, kicking and clubbing of Goode (A3, A4).

Goode was not killed or reported harmed by the crowd; he was committed without bail and later arraigned for trial (A1, A7, A11). The crowd's cries were a threat by a group of unstated size acting on the killing of a policeman (A1).

Only the Washington Critic's brief New York dispatch reports the lynch cries at the transfer (A1); other reports corroborate a pursuing crowd at the arrest (A2, A7, A8) but none of the fuller New York reports mentions the crowd at the Tombs (A3, A4).

accounts.label: New York dispatch on the transfer
accounts.gist: As Goode was taken from the Old Slip station to the Tombs, a crowd surrounded him yelling "Lynch him" and "Kill the black hound"; he was committed without bail.

accounts.label: Masterson and police witnesses
accounts.gist: Goode insulted Masterson; North slapped and kicked him; Goode came back, a scuffle followed, and he stabbed North twice in the throat.

accounts.label: Goode's own account
accounts.gist: He spoke to no woman; North struck him with his club, kicked him and struck him without cause; he ran away and had no knife.

accounts.label: Police captain
accounts.gist: Capt. Caffrey said North should have arrested Goode rather than slap, kick and club him, and that Goode probably mistook Masterson for someone employed by the janitor.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The Freeman said the policeman clubbed a man he should have arrested and that the man acted largely in self-defense, but left judgment to the courts.

framing.detail: Headline 'Lynch Law Sought in New York'; reports the crowd's cries without comment and calls Goode 'the negro' who 'killed Policeman North'.

The Sun's first report, 'Murder of a Policeman ... He Wanted to be Treated Like a White Man', called Goode 'a surly colored man' and a 'low-browed black negro'; its next report printed his denial and the captain's blame of North.
The New York Dispatch headlined 'The Club of a Hasty Policeman, and the Knife of a Negro' and said the evidence showed the officer provoked the crime.
The Narragansett Herald's wire account headlined that 'a Colored Janitor Insults Her' and called Masterson 'the unfortunate cause of the tragedy'.
The New York Freeman's 'The Colored Murderer' condemned the policeman's clubbing and police overreach while urging Black men to obey the law; it did not mention the crowd.
